wm1ac/wm1ac-practice-questions.title: WM1AC practice questions
wm1ac/wm1ac-practice-questions.content:
Test-style questions covering Weeks 1–3, with my own numbers. Try each one before opening the answer. Use radians unless the question says otherwise.


                  
                  Before you start 
                  
                

Decide first: differentiate, integrate, or constant-acceleration equations? (See the table in Calculus for kinematics.)


Maths
1. \mathbf a = 3\mathbf i - 2\mathbf j + \mathbf k and \mathbf b = \mathbf i + 4\mathbf j - 2\mathbf k. Find \mathbf a \cdot \mathbf b, the angle between them, and \mathbf a \times \mathbf b.


                  
                  Answer 
                  
                

\mathbf a \cdot \mathbf b = 3 - 8 - 2 = -7 · \cos\theta = -7/(\sqrt{14}\sqrt{21}) → \theta = 114°
\mathbf a \times \mathbf b = (4 - 4)\mathbf i - (-6 - 1)\mathbf j + (12 + 2)\mathbf k = 7\mathbf j + 14\mathbf k


2. A 40 N force acts along +z at the point (0.2, 0.1, 0) m. Find its moment about the origin.


                  
                  Answer 
                  
                

\mathbf M = \mathbf r \times \mathbf F = (0.1 \times 40)\mathbf i - (0.2 \times 40)\mathbf j = 4\mathbf i - 8\mathbf j N m


Particles
3. A slider’s position is s = 4t^3 - 6t^2 + 1 m. Find its velocity and acceleration at t = 2 s, and when it’s momentarily at rest.


                  
                  Answer 
                  
                

v = 12t^2 - 12t → v(2) = 24 m/s · a = 24t - 12 → a(2) = 36 m/s²
v = 12t(t - 1) = 0 at t = 0 and t = 1 s


4. A cart speeds up uniformly from 2 m/s to 8 m/s over 15 m. Find its acceleration and how long it takes.


                  
                  Answer 
                  
                

64 = 4 + 2a(15) → a = 2 m/s² · t = (8 - 2)/2 = 3 s


5. A particle has a = 2t m/s², starting at v = 1 m/s and s = 0. Find v and s at t = 3 s.


                  
                  Answer 
                  
                

v = 1 + t^2 = 10 m/s · s = t + t^3/3 = 3 + 9 = 12 m


6. A wheel of radius 0.15 m starts from rest with \alpha = 4 rad/s². After 2 s, find the speed and total acceleration of a point on its rim.


                  
                  Answer 
                  
                

\omega = 8 rad/s · v = 1.2 m/s · a_t = 0.6, a_n = 64 \times 0.15 = 9.6 m/s² · a = 9.62 m/s²


Rigid bodies and mechanisms
7. A motor at 1200 rpm brakes uniformly to rest in 5 s. Find α and the number of revolutions it makes while stopping.


                  
                  Answer 
                  
                

\omega_0 = 125.7 rad/s · \alpha = -25.1 rad/s² · \theta = \tfrac12 \times 125.7 \times 5 = 314 rad = 50 rev


8. A motor at 3000 rpm has a 12 mm (radius) pinion driving a 60 mm gear. A 40 mm pulley on the same shaft drives a 100 mm pulley by belt. Find the output speed.


                  
                  Answer 
                  
                

Gear: 3000 \times 12/60 = 600 rpm · Belt: 600 \times 40/100 =  240 rpm


9. A hydraulic cylinder forms the third side of a triangle whose other two sides are fixed at 1.2 m and 0.8 m. The angle between them is 60° and opening at 0.5 rad/s. Find the cylinder’s length and how fast it’s extending.


                  
                  Answer 
                  
                

s^2 = 1.44 + 0.64 - 1.92\cos60° = 1.12 → s = 1.06 m
2s\dot s = 2(1.2)(0.8)\sin\theta\,\dot\theta → \dot s = \dfrac{0.96 \times 0.866 \times 0.5}{1.06} = 0.393 m/s


10. A slider-crank has crank OA = 0.15 m turning at 10 rad/s anticlockwise and rod AB = 0.4 m, with slider B on the horizontal line through O. At the instant the crank is vertical (A directly above O), find the rod’s angular velocity and B’s velocity.


                  
                  Answer 
                  
                

\mathbf v_A = \boldsymbol\omega \times \mathbf r_{A/O} = 10\mathbf k \times 0.15\mathbf j = -1.5\mathbf i m/s
\mathbf r_{B/A} = 0.371\mathbf i - 0.15\mathbf j · v_B\mathbf i = -1.5\mathbf i + \omega_{AB}(0.15\mathbf i + 0.371\mathbf j)
\mathbf j: 0 = 0.371\,\omega_{AB} → \omega_{AB} = 0 · \mathbf i: v_B = -1.5 m/s
At this instant the rod is only translating, so B moves at A’s speed, 1.5 m/s to the left.


Short written answers
11. Give one example each of translation, fixed-axis rotation and general plane motion in a slider-crank.


                  
                  Answer 
                  
                

Slider: translation · crank: fixed-axis rotation · connecting rod: general plane motion.


12. Why do two meshing gears share a tangential velocity but not an angular velocity?


                  
                  Answer 
                  
                

Their teeth move together at the contact point, so the rim speeds r\omega are equal. Different radii then need different ω.

wm1ac/week-1/calculus-for-kinematics.title: Calculus for kinematics
wm1ac/week-1/calculus-for-kinematics.content:
The idea
Kinematics is calculus with physical meaning. Differentiating position gives velocity, and velocity gives acceleration. Integrating goes the other way. Most of the module is choosing which direction to go.
v = \frac{ds}{dt} \qquad a = \frac{dv}{dt} = \frac{d^2s}{dt^2} \qquad \text{(a dot means } \tfrac{d}{dt}\text{: } \dot s = v,\ \ddot s = a\text{)}
Differentiation rules






























RuleFormulaExamplePower\dfrac{d}{dx}x^n = nx^{n-1}\dfrac{d}{dt}(4t^3) = 12t^2Product(uv)' = u'v + uv'\dfrac{d}{dx}(x^2\cos x) = 2x\cos x - x^2\sin xQuotient\left(\dfrac{u}{v}\right)' = \dfrac{u'v - uv'}{v^2}Chain\dfrac{dy}{dx} = \dfrac{dy}{du}\cdot\dfrac{du}{dx}\dfrac{d}{dx}e^{2x} = 2e^{2x}
Integration
The reverse of differentiation, and the area under a curve.

Indefinite (no limits): always add +\,c, then find c from a known condition, like the starting velocity.
Definite (limits): no c. \int_0^2 2x\,dx = [x^2]_0^2 = 4.

Separating the differential is how every kinematics formula is built:
v = \frac{ds}{dt} \;\Rightarrow\; ds = v\,dt \;\Rightarrow\; \int_{s_0}^{s} ds = \int_0^t v\,dt
Techniques you’ll meet: substitution (\int\cos 3x\,dx = \tfrac13\sin 3x + c), by parts (\int u\,dv = uv - \int v\,du) and partial fractions.
Worked example
A robot arm joint has angular acceleration \alpha = 6t rad/s², starting at \omega_0 = 2 rad/s and \theta_0 = 0. Find \omega and \theta at t = 2 s.


                  
                  Answer 
                  
                

\omega = \omega_0 + \int_0^t 6t\,dt = 2 + 3t^2 → \omega(2) = 14 rad/s
\theta = \int_0^t (2 + 3t^2)\,dt = 2t + t^3 → \theta(2) = 12 rad
The starting values become the lower limits, so no +\,c is needed.


Which way to go?

























You’re givenDos(t) or \theta(t)Differentiate for v and aa(t) or \alpha(t)Integrate, using the starting valuesa as a function of positionUse v\,dv = a\,ds (or \omega\,d\omega = \alpha\,d\theta)Constant aUse the constant-acceleration equations (Rectilinear motion)
Check yourself


                  
                  1. s = 5t^2 - 2t. What's a?
                  
                

v = 10t - 2, so a = 10 m/s², constant.




                  
                  2. v = 3t^2 m/s and s(0) = 1 m. Find s(2).
                  
                

s = 1 + t^3, so s(2) = 9 m.

wm1ac/week-1/rectilinear-motion.title: Rectilinear motion
wm1ac/week-1/rectilinear-motion.content:
The idea
The simplest motion: a particle moving along a straight line. Everything is one-dimensional, so position, velocity and acceleration are just numbers with signs. It’s the template for everything that follows, from curves to rotating bodies.
The definitions






























QuantityDefinitionNotePosition sDistance from a fixed origin, with a signDisplacement \Delta sChange in positionNot the same as distance travelledVelocity vv = \dfrac{ds}{dt}Its sign shows directionAcceleration aa = \dfrac{dv}{dt}Negative a isn’t always “slowing down”: it depends on the sign of v
Distance vs displacement: if something goes forward 5 m and back 1 m, the displacement is 4 m but the distance travelled is 6 m. Find where v = 0 (where it turns round) and add up each leg.
Constant acceleration
Only when a is constant:
v = v_0 + at \qquad s = s_0 + v_0t + \tfrac12at^2 \qquad v^2 = v_0^2 + 2a(s - s_0)
If a changes with time, integrate instead (see Calculus for kinematics).
Worked examples
1. A delivery robot speeds up from 0.5 m/s at a constant 0.8 m/s² for 3 s. Final speed and distance?


                  
                  Answer 
                  
                

v = 0.5 + 0.8 \times 3 = 2.9 m/s
s = 0.5 \times 3 + \tfrac12 \times 0.8 \times 3^2 = 1.5 + 3.6 = 5.1 m
Check: v^2 = 0.25 + 2 \times 0.8 \times 5.1 = 8.41 → v = 2.9 ✓


2. A slider’s position is s = 2t^3 - 9t^2 + 12t m. When does it stop, and how far does it travel in the first 3 s?


                  
                  Answer 
                  
                

v = 6t^2 - 18t + 12 = 6(t - 1)(t - 2), so it stops at t = 1 s and t = 2 s.
a = 12t - 18, which is zero at 1.5 s.
s(0) = 0, s(1) = 5, s(2) = 4, s(3) = 9 m.
Distance = 5 + 1 + 5 =  11 m, but the displacement is only 9 m.


Common mistakes

Using the constant-acceleration equations when a depends on t.
Giving displacement when the question asks for distance.
Dropping signs: pick a positive direction and stick to it.

Check yourself


                  
                  1. A cart moving at 3 m/s brakes at a constant 1.5 m/s². Stopping distance? 
                  
                

0 = 9 - 2(1.5)s → s = 3 m.

wm1ac/week-1/vectors.title: Vectors
wm1ac/week-1/vectors.content:
The idea
A vector has a size and a direction: position, velocity, force. Mechanics is full of them, and two ways of multiplying them do most of the work: the dot product (how much of one points along the other) and the cross product (turning effect, like a moment).

Writing vectors

Components: \mathbf v = a\mathbf i + b\mathbf j + c\mathbf k, where \mathbf i, \mathbf j, \mathbf k are unit vectors along x, y, z.
Magnitude: |\mathbf v| = \sqrt{a^2 + b^2 + c^2}
Direction (2D): \theta = \tan^{-1}(b/a). Check the quadrant.
Unit vector: \hat{\mathbf v} = \mathbf v / |\mathbf v|, length 1.
Add, subtract and scale component by component.

Dot product (gives a number)
\mathbf a \cdot \mathbf b = a_xb_x + a_yb_y + a_zb_z = |\mathbf a||\mathbf b|\cos\theta

Use it to find the angle between two vectors.
Perpendicular vectors have \mathbf a \cdot \mathbf b = 0.
The component of a along b is \mathbf a \cdot \hat{\mathbf b}. That’s how you resolve a force along a direction.

Cross product (gives a vector)
\mathbf a \times \mathbf b = \begin{vmatrix} \mathbf i & \mathbf j & \mathbf k \\ a_x & a_y & a_z \\ b_x & b_y & b_z \end{vmatrix} \qquad |\mathbf a \times \mathbf b| = |\mathbf a||\mathbf b|\sin\theta

The result is perpendicular to both, with direction from the right-hand rule.
Order matters: \mathbf a \times \mathbf b = -\,\mathbf b \times \mathbf a.
Main use: the moment of a force, \mathbf M = \mathbf r \times \mathbf F, with \mathbf r first.

Worked example
\mathbf a = 2\mathbf i + 3\mathbf j - \mathbf k, \mathbf b = \mathbf i - \mathbf j + 4\mathbf k. Find \mathbf a \cdot \mathbf b, the angle between them, and \mathbf a \times \mathbf b.


                  
                  Answer 
                  
                

\mathbf a \cdot \mathbf b = 2 - 3 - 4 = -5. |\mathbf a| = \sqrt{14}, |\mathbf b| = \sqrt{18}.
\cos\theta = \dfrac{-5}{\sqrt{14}\sqrt{18}} = -0.315 → \theta = 108.4°
\mathbf a \times \mathbf b = (3\cdot4 - (-1)(-1))\mathbf i - (2\cdot4 - (-1)\cdot1)\mathbf j + (2(-1) - 3\cdot1)\mathbf k = 11\mathbf i - 9\mathbf j - 5\mathbf k
Check it’s perpendicular to \mathbf a: 22 - 27 + 5 = 0 ✓


Common mistakes

Forgetting the minus sign on the \mathbf j term of the cross product.
Swapping the order in \mathbf r \times \mathbf F, which flips the moment’s direction.
Using degrees mode when the question is in radians, or the other way round.

Check yourself


                  
                  1. A 50 N force acts in the +y direction at a point 0.3 m along x from a pivot. Moment? 
                  
                

\mathbf M = 0.3\mathbf i \times 50\mathbf j = 15\mathbf k N m: 15 N m anticlockwise about z.




                  
                  2. Are 3\mathbf i + 4\mathbf j and -4\mathbf i + 3\mathbf j perpendicular?
                  
                

Yes: -12 + 12 = 0.

wm1ac/week-2/curvilinear-and-circular-mo.title: Curvilinear and circular motion
wm1ac/week-2/curvilinear-and-circular-mo.content:
The idea
On a curved path, velocity and acceleration become vectors. The velocity always points along the path (tangent to it). The acceleration generally doesn’t, because it’s doing two jobs: changing the speed and changing the direction.
Position, velocity and acceleration as vectors
In x–y components:
\mathbf r = x\mathbf i + y\mathbf j \qquad \mathbf v = \dot x\mathbf i + \dot y\mathbf j \qquad \mathbf a = \ddot x\mathbf i + \ddot y\mathbf j
Magnitudes come from Pythagoras, e.g. v = \sqrt{\dot x^2 + \dot y^2}.
Averages: \mathbf v_{avg} = \Delta\mathbf r / \Delta t uses the straight-line displacement, not the distance along the curve.
Circular motion
For a point moving round a circle of radius r (angle \theta in radians):

s = r\theta \qquad v = r\omega \qquad a_t = r\alpha \qquad a_n = \frac{v^2}{r} = \omega^2 r \qquad a = \sqrt{a_t^2 + a_n^2}

Tangential a_t changes the speed.
Normal a_n, pointing to the centre, changes the direction. Even at constant speed, a_n \neq 0.
Angular versions of the constant-acceleration equations:
\omega = \omega_0 + \alpha t \qquad \theta = \theta_0 + \omega_0t + \tfrac12\alpha t^2 \qquad \omega^2 = \omega_0^2 + 2\alpha(\theta - \theta_0)

Conversions: 1 rev = 2\pi rad · rpm × \dfrac{2\pi}{60} = rad/s
Worked examples
1. A particle’s position is \mathbf r = 2t^2\mathbf i + 3t\mathbf j m. Find its speed and acceleration at t = 2 s.


                  
                  Answer 
                  
                

\mathbf v = 4t\mathbf i + 3\mathbf j = 8\mathbf i + 3\mathbf j → v = \sqrt{64 + 9} = 8.54 m/s
\mathbf a = 4\mathbf i → a = 4 m/s², pointing along x


2. A robot wheel of radius 0.25 m spins at 12 rad/s and is speeding up at 5 rad/s². Find the speed and acceleration of a point on its rim.


                  
                  Answer 
                  
                

v = 0.25 \times 12 = 3 m/s
a_t = 0.25 \times 5 = 1.25 m/s², a_n = 12^2 \times 0.25 = 36 m/s²
a = \sqrt{1.25^2 + 36^2} = 36.0 m/s². The normal part dominates.


Common mistakes

Using degrees in s = r\theta or v = r\omega. They only work in radians.
Forgetting a_n when the speed is constant.
Using distance instead of displacement for average velocity.

Check yourself


                  
                  1. A point at 0.1 m from an axle turning at 600 rpm. Speed and normal acceleration? 
                  
                

\omega = 600 \times 2\pi/60 = 62.8 rad/s, v = 6.28 m/s, a_n = 62.8^2 \times 0.1 = 395 m/s².

wm1ac/week-2/implicit-differentiation.title: Implicit differentiation
wm1ac/week-2/implicit-differentiation.content:
The idea
In a mechanism, the geometry ties positions together, e.g. “these two sides and this angle make a triangle”. You often can’t rearrange that into y = f(x), and you don’t need to. Differentiate both sides as they stand, using the chain rule on anything that depends on time. That turns a position equation into a velocity equation in one step.
The rule
Anything that changes with time gets the chain rule:
\frac{d}{dt}\big(x^2\big) = 2x\,\dot x \qquad \frac{d}{dt}\big(\cos\theta\big) = -\sin\theta\,\dot\theta \qquad \frac{d}{dt}\big(s^2\big) = 2s\,\dot s
Constants (fixed link lengths) differentiate to zero. Products need the product rule, which you’ll need again on the second differentiation:
\frac{d}{dt}\big(s\,\dot s\big) = \dot s^2 + s\,\ddot s
The recipe for mechanisms

Write the geometry: Pythagoras, trig, or the cosine rule c^2 = a^2 + b^2 - 2ab\cos C.
Differentiate with respect to time → velocities (\dot s, \dot\theta = \omega).
Differentiate again → accelerations (\ddot s, \ddot\theta = \alpha).
Put in the numbers at the instant you care about. Watch the signs: a length that’s getting shorter has negative \dot s.

Worked example
A 5 m ladder leans against a wall. Its foot slides away from the wall at 0.5 m/s. How fast is the top sliding down when the foot is 3 m out?


                  
                  Answer 
                  
                

Geometry: x^2 + y^2 = 25. When x = 3, y = 4.
Differentiate: 2x\dot x + 2y\dot y = 0 → \dot y = -\dfrac{x\dot x}{y} = -\dfrac{3 \times 0.5}{4} = -0.375 m/s
The top slides down at 0.375 m/s.


This is exactly the same maths as a robot’s linear actuator pushing a link, or the A2 slider-crank.
Common mistakes

Forgetting the \dot x (the chain rule part) on each term.
Substituting numbers before differentiating. Differentiate the general equation first.
Using \dot s = 0 when the rate is constant. It’s \ddot s that’s zero.

Check yourself


                  
                  1. Differentiate y = 0.2\cos\theta with respect to time, twice.
                  
                

\dot y = -0.2\sin\theta\,\dot\theta, \ddot y = -0.2\cos\theta\,\dot\theta^2 - 0.2\sin\theta\,\ddot\theta.

wm1ac/week-2/rigid-body-rotation.title: Rigid body rotation
wm1ac/week-2/rigid-body-rotation.content:
The idea
Once a body’s size and shape matter (gears, cranks, linkages), it can’t be treated as a single point. In flat (planar) mechanisms, a rigid body can only move in three ways.

























TypeWhat happensIn a slider-crankTranslationEvery line on the body stays parallel to itself. Straight paths (rectilinear) or curved ones (curvilinear)The slider (piston)Rotation about a fixed axisEvery point moves in a circle round the axisThe crankGeneral plane motionTranslation and rotation at onceThe connecting rod

Translation
Every point has the same velocity and acceleration. Treat the whole body as a particle.
Rotation about a fixed axis
\omega = \frac{d\theta}{dt}\ \text{(rad/s)} \qquad \alpha = \frac{d\omega}{dt} = \frac{d^2\theta}{dt^2}\ \text{(rad/s}^2\text{)}
A point at radius r: v = \omega r, a_t = \alpha r, a_n = \omega^2r (see Curvilinear and circular motion).

Constant α: use the angular constant-acceleration equations.
α varies with time: integrate, \int d\omega = \int\alpha\,dt, then \int d\theta = \int\omega\,dt.
α depends on angle: use \omega\,d\omega = \alpha\,d\theta.

A smooth pin support stops a body moving sideways or up and down, but lets it rotate freely.
Worked examples
1. A motor spins up uniformly from rest to 3000 rpm in 2 s. Find α and how many revolutions it makes.


                  
                  Answer 
                  
                

\omega = 3000 \times 2\pi/60 = 314.2 rad/s, so \alpha = 314.2/2 = 157.1 rad/s²
\theta = \tfrac12 \times 157.1 \times 2^2 = 314.2 rad = 50 rev


2. A gear starts at 10 rad/s with \alpha = 6t rad/s². Find ω and θ after 2 s.


                  
                  Answer 
                  
                

\omega = 10 + 3t^2 = 22 rad/s
\theta = 10t + t^3 = 28 rad


Check yourself


                  
                  1. Which type of motion does a lift car have? 
                  
                

Translation (rectilinear): every point moves the same way.




                  
                  2. A flywheel slows from 50 to 20 rad/s in 6 s at a constant rate. α? 
                  
                

\alpha = (20 - 50)/6 = -5 rad/s².

wm1ac/week-3/absolute-motion-analysis.title: Absolute motion analysis
wm1ac/week-3/absolute-motion-analysis.content:
The idea
For a mechanism like a slider-crank, write one equation for the position of the part you care about in terms of the input angle. Then differentiate it with respect to time once for velocity and again for acceleration. It’s called “absolute” because every position is measured from a fixed origin.
The method

Geometry: write the position (e.g. the slider’s x) in terms of the crank angle \theta, using trig or the cosine rule.
Differentiate with respect to time → velocity. Every \theta term picks up a \dot\theta = \omega.
Differentiate again (product rule) → acceleration, with \ddot\theta = \alpha.
Substitute the values at the instant asked for, and check the signs make sense physically.

Worked example: a Scotch yoke
A crank of radius r = 0.1 m drives a slotted yoke, whose position is x = r\cos\theta. The crank turns at a constant 20 rad/s. Find the yoke’s velocity and acceleration at \theta = 30°.


                  
                  Answer 
                  
                

x = 0.1\cos\theta
\dot x = -0.1\sin\theta\,\dot\theta → at 30°: -0.1 \times 0.5 \times 20 =  −1.0 m/s (moving towards −x)
\ddot x = -0.1\cos\theta\,\dot\theta^2 - 0.1\sin\theta\,\ddot\theta. Constant ω means \ddot\theta = 0:
\ddot x = -0.1 \times 0.866 \times 400 =  −34.6 m/s²


The yoke moves in simple harmonic motion, which is why this mechanism is used in some pumps and shakers.
When the geometry is a triangle
For a hydraulic cylinder pushing a link, the cylinder length s and the link angle are tied by the cosine rule:
s^2 = a^2 + b^2 - 2ab\cos\theta \;\Rightarrow\; 2s\dot s = 2ab\sin\theta\,\dot\theta
Given the cylinder’s extension rate \dot s, solve for \dot\theta. Differentiate again for \ddot\theta, remembering that a constant rate means \ddot s = 0, not \dot s = 0.
Common mistakes

Plugging in numbers before differentiating.
Losing the second term of the product rule on the second derivative.
Sign of the velocity: decide which way is positive and check your answer agrees with the picture.

Check yourself


                  
                  1. Same Scotch yoke, but at θ = 90°. Velocity and acceleration? 
                  
                

\dot x = -0.1 \times 1 \times 20 = -2 m/s (its fastest), \ddot x = 0 (cos 90° = 0).

wm1ac/week-3/gear-trains-and-belt-drives.title: Gear trains and belt drives
wm1ac/week-3/gear-trains-and-belt-drives.content:
The idea
Gears, belts and cords pass motion from one body to another. The key is what’s shared at the contact: where two gears mesh (or a belt grips a pulley without slipping), the touching points move together, so they have the same speed along the contact.

The rules
Meshing gears, and belts or cords with no slip:
r_A\omega_A = r_B\omega_B \qquad r_A\alpha_A = r_B\alpha_B
Things on the same shaft share \omega and \alpha.

A small gear driving a big one slows the output and (ideally) multiplies the torque by the same ratio.
Meshing gears turn opposite ways. A belt keeps the same direction (unless it’s crossed).
To go from rotation to a load on a cord or drum: v = r\omega, a = r\alpha.

Mechanism vocabulary

A link is a rigid body with at least two attachment points (nodes). Two nodes = binary, three = ternary.
Full joints allow one degree of freedom: a pin (revolute) joint allows rotation only; a slider (prismatic) joint allows translation only.

Worked examples
1. A motor’s 20 mm pinion turns at 1500 rpm and drives an 80 mm gear. Output speed and ideal torque ratio?


                  
                  Answer 
                  
                

\omega_B = 1500 \times \dfrac{20}{80} = 375 rpm, turning the opposite way.
The torque is multiplied by 80/20 = 4 (ignoring losses).


2. Gear A (r = 50 mm) starts from rest with \alpha_A = 3 rad/s² and drives gear B (r = 150 mm). A 100 mm drum on B’s shaft winds up a cable lifting a load. Find the load’s acceleration and speed after 4 s.


                  
                  Answer 
                  
                

Mesh: \alpha_B = \dfrac{50 \times 3}{150} = 1 rad/s². The drum shares B’s shaft, so \alpha_D = 1 rad/s².
a_{load} = r_D\alpha_D = 0.1 \times 1 = 0.1 m/s²
v = 0 + 0.1 \times 4 = 0.4 m/s


The pattern for any drive problem

Find what’s shared at each contact: the same tangential v and a.
Convert between linear and angular with r at each step.
Use the constant-α equations if α is constant.

Common mistakes

Using diameters on one side and radii on the other. Either works, but be consistent.
Assuming meshing gears have the same ω. They have the same rim speed.
Forgetting gears on a shared shaft have the same ω even if their radii differ.

Check yourself


                  
                  1. A 0.15 m pulley at 7.1 rad/s drives a 0.4 m pulley by belt. Speed of the second pulley's rim? 
                  
                

Same as the first: 0.15 \times 7.1 = 1.07 m/s. Its ω is 1.07/0.4 = 2.66 rad/s.

wm1ac/week-3/relative-motion-analysis.title: Relative motion analysis
wm1ac/week-3/relative-motion-analysis.content:
The idea
For a body in general plane motion (like a connecting rod), the motion of any point B equals the motion of another point A plus the motion caused by the body rotating about A. You don’t need a position equation; you work directly with vectors at the instant you care about.
The equations
\mathbf v_B = \mathbf v_A + \boldsymbol\omega \times \mathbf r_{B/A}
\mathbf a_B = \mathbf a_A + \boldsymbol\alpha \times \mathbf r_{B/A} - \omega^2\,\mathbf r_{B/A}

\mathbf r_{B/A} is the vector from A to B.
For flat motion, \boldsymbol\omega = \omega\mathbf k and \boldsymbol\alpha = \alpha\mathbf k (anticlockwise positive).
Handy: \mathbf k \times \mathbf i = \mathbf j and \mathbf k \times \mathbf j = -\mathbf i.
The -\omega^2\mathbf r_{B/A} term is the normal (centripetal) part; \boldsymbol\alpha \times \mathbf r_{B/A} is the tangential part.

The method

Pick A as a point whose motion you know (e.g. a pin on a crank, or a slider).
Write \mathbf r_{B/A} in components.
Write what you know about \mathbf v_B‘s direction (e.g. a slider can only move along its guide).
Expand, then match the \mathbf i and \mathbf j components: two equations, two unknowns.
Repeat for acceleration, using the ω you just found.

Worked example
A 0.5 m rod AB has end A sliding along the floor to the right at 2 m/s (constant) and end B sliding down a vertical wall. The rod is at 60° to the floor. Find the rod’s ω and α, and B’s velocity and acceleration.


                  
                  Answer 
                  
                

\mathbf r_{B/A} = -0.5\cos60°\,\mathbf i + 0.5\sin60°\,\mathbf j = -0.25\mathbf i + 0.433\mathbf j
Velocity: v_B\mathbf j = 2\mathbf i + \omega\mathbf k \times(-0.25\mathbf i + 0.433\mathbf j) = 2\mathbf i - 0.433\omega\,\mathbf i - 0.25\omega\,\mathbf j
\mathbf i: 0 = 2 - 0.433\omega → \omega = 4.62 rad/s (anticlockwise)
\mathbf j: v_B = -0.25 \times 4.62 = -1.15 m/s (moving down)
Acceleration (\mathbf a_A = 0, \omega^2 = 21.3):
a_B\mathbf j = \alpha\mathbf k \times \mathbf r_{B/A} - 21.3(-0.25\mathbf i + 0.433\mathbf j)
\mathbf i: 0 = -0.433\alpha + 5.33 → \alpha = 12.3 rad/s²
\mathbf j: a_B = -0.25 \times 12.3 - 21.3 \times 0.433 = -12.3 m/s²
Check with Implicit differentiation: x^2 + y^2 = 0.25 gives \dot y = -x\dot x/y = -0.25 \times 2/0.433 = -1.15 m/s ✓


Common mistakes

Using \mathbf r_{A/B} instead of \mathbf r_{B/A}, which flips every sign.
Getting the cross products wrong: \mathbf k \times \mathbf j = -\mathbf i.
Forgetting the -\omega^2\mathbf r term in the acceleration.

Check yourself


                  
                  1. In the example, why is B's acceleration non-zero even though A moves at constant speed? 
                  
                

The rod’s angle keeps changing, so ω changes (α ≠ 0) and there’s a centripetal term. B’s motion is constrained to the wall, so it speeds up as it falls.


Next
Put it all together in the Slider-crank worked example: a test-style question with a speeding-up crank and a horizontal slider.

wm1ac/week-3/slider-crank-worked-example.title: Slider-crank worked example
wm1ac/week-3/slider-crank-worked-example.content:
Why this one
One question that uses every Week 1–3 skill: geometry with Pythagoras, position vectors, cross products, relative velocity, relative acceleration (tangential and normal parts), a sliding constraint, and reading the signs of the answers. It’s the same kind of mechanism as the A2 rig, and it’s set up like a test question. Try each part before opening the answer.
Theory: Relative motion analysis · Absolute motion analysis · Rigid body rotation
The question
A slider-crank has crank OA = 0.2 m pinned at O and connecting rod AB = 0.5 m. Slider B moves along a horizontal guide level with O. At the instant shown, the crank is at 60° above the horizontal and is turning anticlockwise at ω = 8 rad/s, and speeding up at α = 30 rad/s².

Find:

(a) The position of B, and the position vector \mathbf r_{B/A}
(b) The velocity of A
(c) The angular velocity of rod AB and the velocity of slider B
(d) The acceleration of A
(e) The angular acceleration of rod AB and the acceleration of slider B
(f) Is the slider speeding up or slowing down? Describe the motion of each link.



                  
                  What's different from the lecture example 
                  
                

Here the crank is speeding up, so A has a tangential acceleration as well as a normal one. The slider moves horizontally, so the constraint kills the j parts instead of the i parts. And the answers come out negative, so you have to interpret the signs.


Set-up
Origin at O, i right, j up, k out of the page, anticlockwise positive. Cross products you need (not on the formula sheet):
\mathbf k\times\mathbf i = \mathbf j \qquad \mathbf k\times\mathbf j = -\mathbf i \qquad\Rightarrow\qquad \omega\mathbf k\times(x\,\mathbf i + y\,\mathbf j) = -\omega y\,\mathbf i + \omega x\,\mathbf j


                  
                  (a) Geometry 
                  
                

A: \mathbf r_A = 0.2\cos60°\,\mathbf i + 0.2\sin60°\,\mathbf j = 0.1\,\mathbf i + 0.1732\,\mathbf j
B is on the line through O, so it’s 0.1732 m below A. Pythagoras on the rod:
\text{horizontal gap} = \sqrt{0.5^2 - 0.1732^2} = \sqrt{0.22} = 0.4690\ \text{m}
So x_B = 0.1 + 0.4690 = \mathbf{0.569\ m} from O, and
\mathbf r_{B/A} = 0.4690\,\mathbf i - 0.1732\,\mathbf j
The rod sits at \tan^{-1}(0.1732/0.4690) = 20.3° below horizontal.




                  
                  (b) Velocity of A 
                  
                

\mathbf v_A = \boldsymbol\omega_{OA}\times\mathbf r_A = 8\mathbf k\times(0.1\,\mathbf i + 0.1732\,\mathbf j) = -1.386\,\mathbf i + 0.8\,\mathbf j\ \text{m/s}
Size = 8 \times 0.2 = 1.6 m/s, perpendicular to OA (up and to the left), as it should be for an anticlockwise crank.




                  
                  (c) Angular velocity of AB, velocity of B 
                  
                

\mathbf v_B = \mathbf v_A + \boldsymbol\omega_{AB}\times\mathbf r_{B/A}
B can only move along the guide, so \mathbf v_B = v_B\,\mathbf i (no j part).
\omega_{AB}\mathbf k\times(0.4690\,\mathbf i - 0.1732\,\mathbf j) = 0.1732\,\omega_{AB}\,\mathbf i + 0.4690\,\omega_{AB}\,\mathbf j
v_B\,\mathbf i = (-1.386 + 0.1732\,\omega_{AB})\,\mathbf i + (0.8 + 0.4690\,\omega_{AB})\,\mathbf j
j (one unknown, so do it first): 0 = 0.8 + 0.4690\,\omega_{AB} → \omega_{AB} = \mathbf{-1.706\ rad/s}, i.e. 1.71 rad/s clockwise
i: v_B = -1.386 + 0.1732(-1.706) = \mathbf{-1.681\ m/s}, i.e. 1.68 m/s to the left




                  
                  (d) Acceleration of A 
                  
                

The crank is speeding up, so A has both parts:
\mathbf a_A = \boldsymbol\alpha_{OA}\times\mathbf r_A - \omega_{OA}^2\,\mathbf r_A
= 30\mathbf k\times(0.1\,\mathbf i + 0.1732\,\mathbf j) - 64(0.1\,\mathbf i + 0.1732\,\mathbf j)
= (-5.196\,\mathbf i + 3\,\mathbf j) - (6.4\,\mathbf i + 11.085\,\mathbf j) = -11.596\,\mathbf i - 8.085\,\mathbf j\ \text{m/s}^2
Check: tangential = 30\times0.2 = 6, normal = 64\times0.2 = 12.8, total =\sqrt{6^2+12.8^2} = 14.1 m/s², and \sqrt{11.596^2 + 8.085^2} = 14.1 ✓




                  
                  (e) Angular acceleration of AB, acceleration of B 
                  
                

\mathbf a_B = \mathbf a_A + \boldsymbol\alpha_{AB}\times\mathbf r_{B/A} - \omega_{AB}^2\,\mathbf r_{B/A}, \qquad \mathbf a_B = a_B\,\mathbf i
Tangential: \alpha_{AB}\mathbf k\times(0.4690\,\mathbf i - 0.1732\,\mathbf j) = 0.1732\,\alpha_{AB}\,\mathbf i + 0.4690\,\alpha_{AB}\,\mathbf j
Normal: -(1.706)^2(0.4690\,\mathbf i - 0.1732\,\mathbf j) = -2.909(0.4690\,\mathbf i - 0.1732\,\mathbf j) = -1.364\,\mathbf i + 0.504\,\mathbf j
j: 0 = -8.085 + 0.4690\,\alpha_{AB} + 0.504 → \alpha_{AB} = \mathbf{16.2\ rad/s^2} anticlockwise
i: a_B = -11.596 + 0.1732(16.16) - 1.364 = \mathbf{-10.2\ m/s^2}, i.e. 10.2 m/s² to the left
Note the square: \omega_{AB}^2 is positive even though \omega_{AB} is negative.




                  
                  (f) Interpreting the answers 
                  
                


v_B and a_B are both negative (both to the left), so the slider is speeding up as it moves left. Same sign means speeding up; opposite signs means slowing down.
\omega_{AB} is clockwise but \alpha_{AB} is anticlockwise, so the rod’s rotation is slowing down at this instant.
Crank OA: fixed-axis rotation about O (revolute joint). Rod AB: general plane motion (translation plus rotation). Slider B: rectilinear translation along a prismatic joint. Pins at O, A and B plus a prismatic joint between the slider and its guide make a four-link chain (ground, crank, rod, slider) with one degree of freedom: set the crank angle and everything else is fixed.



Answers





































Answerx_B0.569 m from O\mathbf v_A-1.386\,\mathbf i + 0.8\,\mathbf j m/s (1.6 m/s)\omega_{AB}1.71 rad/s clockwisev_B1.68 m/s left\mathbf a_A-11.60\,\mathbf i - 8.09\,\mathbf j m/s² (14.1 m/s²)\alpha_{AB}16.2 rad/s² anticlockwisea_B10.2 m/s² left (speeding up)
Common mistakes

Forgetting A’s tangential acceleration. It’s only zero when the crank turns at a constant rate.
Using the wrong constraint. A horizontal slider has no j velocity or acceleration, so the j equation is the one with a single unknown.
Sign of \omega^2. Square the number, including its minus sign: (-1.706)^2 = +2.909.
Getting \mathbf r_{B/A} the wrong way round. It runs from A to B, so here the j part is negative because B is lower than A.
Reporting a negative as a size. Say “1.68 m/s to the left” or “−1.68 i m/s”, not just “−1.68”.

Check yourself


                  
                  1. At what crank angle would the rod have zero angular velocity for an instant? 
                  
                

When the crank points straight up or down (90° or 270°). Then \mathbf v_A is horizontal, the same direction as the slider, so the rod just translates and \omega_{AB} = 0.




                  
                  2. If the crank turned at a constant 8 rad/s instead, which terms in part (d) disappear? 
                  
                

The tangential part, \boldsymbol\alpha_{OA}\times\mathbf r_A. Then \mathbf a_A = -64\,\mathbf r_A = -6.4\,\mathbf i - 11.09\,\mathbf j m/s², pointing straight at O.

wm1ac/index.title: WM1AC · Mechanisms and Machines
wm1ac/index.content:
Block 1 · 15 credits. How things move and why: the kinematics and kinetics of particles, rigid bodies and mechanisms like gear trains and slider-cranks. The maths is taught alongside the mechanics, so each week has a maths topic and an engineering topic that uses it.
Assessment: A1 computer-based test, 30% (week 5, formula sheet provided) · A2 individual lab report on a geared slider-crank, 70% (week 9).
Textbook: Hibbeler, Engineering Mechanics: Dynamics (and Statics), 14th ed.
Week 1: calculus, vectors and straight-line motion

Calculus for kinematics: differentiation and integration, the way mechanics uses them
Vectors: components, dot product and cross product
Matrices and Cramer’s rule (shared with WM1AD)
Rectilinear motion: position, velocity and acceleration in a straight line

Week 2: curves, rotation and implicit differentiation

Curvilinear and circular motion: motion along a curve, tangential and normal acceleration
Rigid body rotation: translation, fixed-axis rotation and general plane motion
Implicit differentiation: differentiating geometry with respect to time

Week 3: mechanisms

Gear trains and belt drives: what’s shared at a contact
Absolute motion analysis: geometry → velocity → acceleration
Relative motion analysis: \mathbf v_B = \mathbf v_A + \boldsymbol\omega \times \mathbf r_{B/A}
Slider-crank worked example: one test-style question that uses every Week 1–3 skill

Coming next
Week 4: forces, moments, static equilibrium, Newton’s second law and centre of mass.
Revision

WM1AC practice questions: test-style questions with hidden worked answers
