wm1ad/wm1ad-practice-questions.title: WM1AD practice questions
wm1ad/wm1ad-practice-questions.content:
Test-style questions covering Weeks 1–3, with my own numbers. Try each one on paper with a calculator before opening the answer. Answers are rounded to 3 significant figures.


                  
                  How to use this page 
                  
                

Time yourself: test questions are usually 5–10 minutes each. Write units on every line, and finish circuit questions with a power balance.


Week 1
1. A 48 V robot drive motor is rated at 360 W. Find the current, the winding resistance as seen from the supply, and the energy used in 15 minutes in kWh.


                  
                  Answer 
                  
                

I = P/V = 360/48 = 7.5 A · R = V/I = 48/7.5 = 6.4\ \Omega · E = 0.36\ \text{kW} \times 0.25\ \text{h} = 0.09 kWh


2. A battery feeds a DC-DC converter (94%), a motor drive (96%) and a motor (88%). The motor delivers 200 W. What power does the battery supply, and how much is lost?


                  
                  Answer 
                  
                

\eta = 0.94 \times 0.96 \times 0.88 = 0.794 · P_{in} = 200/0.794 = 252 W · losses = 51.9 W


3. A 24 V supply feeds R_1 = 3\ \Omega, then 12\ \Omega and 6\ \Omega in parallel, then R_4 = 5\ \Omega, all in series. Find every current and check the power balance.


                  
                  Answer 
                  
                

Parallel pair: 12 \times 6/18 = 4\ \Omega · R_T = 3 + 4 + 5 = 12\ \Omega · I = 2 A
Parallel voltage = 2 \times 4 = 8 V → I_{12} = 0.667 A, I_6 = 1.33 A (sum 2 ✓)
Powers: 12 + 5.33 + 10.7 + 20 = 48 W = 24 \times 2 ✓


4. A Wheatstone bridge has R_1 = 470\ \Omega, R_2 = 1 kΩ and R_3 = 2.2 kΩ. What value of R_4 balances it?


                  
                  Answer 
                  
                

R_4 = R_2R_3/R_1 = 1000 \times 2200/470 = 4.68 kΩ


5. A 10 kΩ NTC thermistor has B = 3435 K. What’s its resistance at 60 °C?


                  
                  Answer 
                  
                

T = 333.15 K · R = 10\,000\exp[3435(1/333.15 - 1/298.15)] = 2.98 kΩ


Week 2
6. Find \det\begin{bmatrix} 2 & -1 & 3 \\ 1 & 4 & 0 \\ -2 & 5 & 1 \end{bmatrix}.


                  
                  Answer 
                  
                

Along row 1: 2(4 - 0) + 1(1 - 0) + 3(5 + 8) = 8 + 1 + 39 =  48


7. A three-mesh circuit (like the one in Mesh analysis) has V_1 = 30 V, V_2 = 10 V, R_1 = 2, R_2 = 5, R_3 = 4, R_4 = 6, R_5 = 3\ \Omega. Write the matrix, find the mesh currents and the current in each shared branch, and check the power balance.


                  
                  Answer 
                  
                

\begin{bmatrix} 7 & -5 & 0 \\ -5 & 15 & -6 \\ 0 & -6 & 9 \end{bmatrix}\begin{bmatrix} I_1 \\ I_2 \\ I_3 \end{bmatrix} = \begin{bmatrix} 30 \\ 0 \\ 10 \end{bmatrix}, \Delta = 468
I_1 = 6.99 A, I_2 = 3.78 A, I_3 = 3.63 A · I_{R2} = 3.21 A, I_{R4} = 0.150 A
Power: \sum I^2R = 246 W = 30 \times 6.99 + 10 \times 3.63 ✓


8. A 5 V supply charges a 470 µF capacitor through 1 kΩ. Find τ, the time to reach 4 V, and the energy stored when it’s full.


                  
                  Answer 
                  
                

\tau = 0.47 s · 4 = 5(1 - e^{-t/0.47}) → t = 0.47\ln 5 = 0.756 s · E = \tfrac12 \times 470\times10^{-6} \times 25 = 5.88 mJ


Week 3
9. A bridge rectifier (V_F = 0.95 V) on 230 V mains carries 3 A RMS into a 6800 µF capacitor. Find the bridge loss, the capacitor’s peak voltage and the ripple.


                  
                  Answer 
                  
                

P = 1.8 \times 0.95 \times 3 = 5.13 W · V_{C,max} = 325.3 - 1.9 = 323 V · \Delta V = 3/(100 \times 0.0068) = 4.41 V


10. An IRFP250 (R_{DS(on)} = 0.075\ \Omega; 14 + 43 ns on, 41 + 33 ns off) switches 36 V at 15 A, 50 kHz. Total loss?


                  
                  Answer 
                  
                

P_{cond} = 0.075 \times 225 = 16.9 W · E_{ON} = 270 \times 57\times10^{-9} = 15.4\ \muJ · E_{OFF} = 270 \times 74\times10^{-9} = 20.0\ \muJ
P_{SW} = 35.4\times10^{-6} \times 50\,000 = 1.77 W · P_{MOSFET} = 18.6 W


11. The MOSFET in Q10 sits on a 3 °C/W heatsink (R_{th1} = 0.7, R_{th2} = 0.24 °C/W) at 35 °C ambient. Find T_J and the safety margin. What heatsink would hold it at 100 °C?


                  
                  Answer 
                  
                

T_J = 35 + 18.6 \times (0.7 + 0.24 + 3) = 108 °C · margin = 100 - 108/175 \times 100 = 38\% ✓
For 100 °C: R_{th3} = 65/18.6 - 0.94 = 2.55 °C/W


12. A buck converter steps 36 V down to 12 V at 3 A, switching at 200 kHz, with 20% current and voltage ripple. Find D, L and C.


                  
                  Answer 
                  
                

D = 1/3 · \Delta I = 0.6 A, \Delta V = 2.4 V
L = 12 \times (2/3)/(200\,000 \times 0.6) = 66.7\ \muH · C \ge 0.6/(8 \times 200\,000 \times 2.4) = 0.156\ \muF


13. A 12 V motor runs from a 24 V battery using PWM. What duty cycle gives it its rated average voltage?


                  
                  Answer 
                  
                

D = 12/24 = 50\%


Short written answers
14. Why would you choose a MOSFET over an IGBT for a 48 V robot drive? (2–3 sentences)


                  
                  Answer 
                  
                

At 48 V a MOSFET has low on-resistance and switches much faster than an IGBT, so it has lower total loss and allows higher PWM frequencies with smaller filter parts. IGBTs only make sense above roughly 700–1000 V.


15. Explain why switching loss becomes important in DC-DC converters.


                  
                  Answer 
                  
                

Switching loss is proportional to frequency. Converters run at 100+ kHz to keep the inductor and capacitor small, so energy lost in each transition happens hundreds of thousands of times a second, and it can match or exceed conduction loss.

wm1ad/week-1/electrical-quantities.title: Electrical quantities
wm1ad/week-1/electrical-quantities.content:
The idea
Everything in this module is built from a handful of quantities. Think of a circuit like water in pipes: charge is the water, current is how fast it flows, voltage is the pressure pushing it, and resistance is how narrow the pipe is.















































QuantitySymbolUnitMeaningChargeQcoulomb (C)Amount of electricityCurrentIampere (A)Charge per second: I = Q/tVoltageVvolt (V)Energy per unit charge, the “push”ResistanceRohm (Ω)Opposition to currentPowerPwatt (W)Energy per secondEnergyEjoule (J) or kWhPower × time
Ohm’s law and resistance
V = IR
The resistance of a wire depends on what it’s made of and its shape:
R = \rho\,\frac{L}{A}
where \rho is the material’s resistivity (Ω m), L the length and A the cross-sectional area. Longer or thinner means more resistance. Resistors are specified by resistance, power rating (how much heat they can take) and tolerance (e.g. ±1%).
Power and energy
Combine P = VI with Ohm’s law and you get three forms. Use whichever matches what you know:
P = VI = I^2R = \frac{V^2}{R} \qquad E = Pt

1 J = 1 W for 1 s. Electricity bills use kWh: 1 kW for 1 hour = 3.6 MJ.
Cost = energy in kWh × price per kWh. Watch the units: W × h gives Wh, so divide by 1000.

Efficiency
No real machine converts all its input power to useful output. The rest becomes heat.
\eta = \frac{P_{out}}{P_{in}} \times 100\% \qquad P_{loss} = P_{in} - P_{out}
Stages in series multiply: a supply (95%) feeding a drive (97%) feeding a motor (92%) gives 0.95 \times 0.97 \times 0.92 = 84.8\%. The overall efficiency is always lower than the worst stage.
Small efficiency gains are worth a lot over time. A machine running 16 h a day, 300 days a year, at 3 kW output, wastes about £640 a year at 85% efficiency but only about £310 at 92% (at £0.25/kWh).
Fuses
A fuse is a wire designed to melt above a set current, opening the circuit before anything overheats. Choose the smallest standard rating above the normal operating current. A 1 kW charger on 240 V draws 4.2 A, so it gets a 5 A fuse.
Worked example
A robot’s 24 V battery supplies a drive motor drawing 4 A for 30 minutes. The motor’s mechanical output is 80 W. Find the power drawn, the charge and energy used, the motor’s resistance as seen from the supply, its efficiency, and a suitable fuse.


                  
                  Answer 
                  
                

P = VI = 24 \times 4 = 96 W
Q = It = 4 \times 1800 = 7200 C
E = Pt = 96 \times 0.5\ \text{h} = 48 Wh = 0.048 kWh = 172.8 kJ
R = V/I = 24/4 = 6\ \Omega
\eta = 80/96 = 83.3\%, so 16 W is lost as heat.
Normal current 4 A → 5 A fuse.


Common mistakes

Mixing up W and Wh. Power is a rate; energy is power × time.
Forgetting to convert minutes to hours (for kWh) or to seconds (for J).
Writing R = I/V instead of V/I. Check the units: Ω = V/A.
Giving a voltage in Ω or a current in C. Units are marked.

Check yourself


                  
                  1. What's the resistance of 10 m of copper wire with a 0.5 mm² cross-section? ( \rho_{Cu} = 1.72\times10^{-8} Ω m)
                  
                

R = 1.72\times10^{-8} \times 10 / (0.5\times10^{-6}) = 0.344\ \Omega. Remember mm² = 10^{-6} m².




                  
                  2. A 2 Ω winding carries 5 A. How much power does it waste? 
                  
                

P = I^2R = 25 \times 2 = 50 W.




                  
                  3. Three stages at 90%, 95% and 85%. Overall efficiency? 
                  
                

0.9 \times 0.95 \times 0.85 = 72.7\%.

wm1ad/week-1/kirchhoff's-laws.title: Kirchhoff's laws
wm1ad/week-1/kirchhoff's-laws.content:
The idea
Two rules let you analyse any circuit. Both are just conservation laws:

KCL (current law): charge can’t pile up at a junction, so current in = current out.
KVL (voltage law): energy is conserved round a loop, so the voltage rises equal the voltage drops.


\text{KCL: } \sum I = 0 \qquad \text{KVL: } \sum V = 0 \text{ round any closed loop}
Sign conventions: count currents into a node as + and out as −. If a current you solve for comes out negative, it simply flows the opposite way to the arrow you drew. Keep the sign and carry on.
Sources in a loop: a source that pushes the same way as the others adds; one turned round subtracts. Three cells of 20, 10 and 20 V with the 10 V reversed give 20 - 10 + 20 = 30 V.
Series and parallel

























SeriesParallelSame for each partCurrentVoltageTotal resistanceR_T = R_1 + R_2 + \dots\dfrac{1}{R_T} = \dfrac{1}{R_1} + \dfrac{1}{R_2} + \dotsTwo resistorsR_T = \dfrac{R_1R_2}{R_1 + R_2} (product over sum)
Voltage divider (two resistors in series): V_{2} = V\,\dfrac{R_2}{R_1 + R_2}
Current divider (two in parallel): I_{2} = I\,\dfrac{R_3}{R_2 + R_3}, the current through one branch uses the other branch’s resistance on top.
The method for any series–parallel circuit

Reduce the network to one total resistance R_T.
Total current I_T = V/R_T.
Work back out: the voltage across each block, then each branch current.
Check KVL (the drops add up to the supply) and KCL (the branches add up to the total).
Check the power balance: the power dissipated in the resistors, \sum I^2R, must equal the power from the sources, \sum VI.

The power balance is the best check there is. If it doesn’t balance, something upstream is wrong.
Worked example
A 12 V supply feeds R_1 = 4\ \Omega in series with R_2 = 6\ \Omega and R_3 = 12\ \Omega in parallel. Find every current and check the power balance.


                  
                  Answer 
                  
                

R_2 \parallel R_3 = \dfrac{6 \times 12}{18} = 4\ \Omega, so R_T = 4 + 4 = 8\ \Omega and I_T = 12/8 = 1.5 A.
V_{R1} = 1.5 \times 4 = 6 V, so the parallel pair gets 12 - 6 = 6 V.
I_2 = 6/6 = 1 A, I_3 = 6/12 = 0.5 A. KCL: 1 + 0.5 = 1.5 ✓
Powers: 1.5^2 \times 4 = 9 W, 1^2 \times 6 = 6 W, 0.5^2 \times 12 = 3 W → total 18 W = 12 \times 1.5 ✓


Common mistakes

Adding parallel resistances directly. Parallel always gives less than the smallest resistor.
In a current divider, putting the branch’s own resistance on top.
Throwing away a negative answer. It’s information: the current flows the other way.

Check yourself


                  
                  1. 10 Ω and 15 Ω in parallel? 
                  
                

\dfrac{150}{25} = 6\ \Omega.




                  
                  2. A 9 V supply across 1 kΩ and 2 kΩ in series. Voltage across the 2 kΩ? 
                  
                

9 \times \dfrac{2}{3} = 6 V.

wm1ad/week-1/power-electronics-overview.title: Power electronics overview
wm1ad/week-1/power-electronics-overview.content:
The idea
A robot’s energy almost never arrives in the form its motors need. Power electronics converts it: AC to DC, one DC voltage to another, DC to AC for motors. This page is the map; the Week 3 guides fill in each piece.
The four conversions






























ConversionCircuitExample in a robotAC → DCRectifierThe charger plugged into the wall (Bridge rectifiers)DC → DCBuck (down) or boost (up) converter48 V battery to 5 V logic (DC-DC converters)DC → ACInverterDriving a brushless motor (Motor drives)AC → ACFrequency converterRare in robotics
The components

































ComponentWhat it doesResistorLimits current, turns energy into heatCapacitorStores energy in an electric field; smooths voltageInductorStores energy in a magnetic field; smooths currentTransformerSteps AC voltage up or down, and isolatesDiodeOne-way valve for currentBJT, MOSFET, IGBTElectronic switches (Power switches)
A MOSFET as a low-side switch
The most common way a microcontroller switches a motor on and off:
 +V ──── motor ──── Drain
                   MOSFET   Gate ──R_G── microcontroller pin
 0 V ─────────────  Source      └─R_PD── 0 V


Main loop: battery + → motor → drain → source → ground. The switch is on the ground side, so it’s a low-side switch.
Gate resistor R_G: limits the current spike that charges the gate.
Pull-down R_{PD}: holds the gate low so the motor stays off if the control pin floats, at power-up or if a wire comes loose.
Common ground: the controller’s ground must connect to the power ground, because the MOSFET responds to gate voltage relative to its source.
Flyback diode across the motor: when the switch turns off, the motor’s inductance tries to keep current flowing. The diode gives it a path, instead of a voltage spike that would kill the MOSFET.

Check yourself


                  
                  1. Why does a motor need a flyback diode but a heater doesn't? 
                  
                

A motor winding is an inductor, which resists sudden changes in current and creates a voltage spike when switched off. A heater is (almost) pure resistance.

wm1ad/week-1/voltage-node-method.title: Voltage node method
wm1ad/week-1/voltage-node-method.content:
The idea
When a circuit has more than one source, simple series–parallel reduction stops working. The node method picks one unknown, the voltage at the main junction, and writes KCL there with every current expressed as \Delta V / R. One equation, one unknown.
The method

Mark the nodes and choose a reference node (ground, 0 V). Every node voltage is measured from it.
Draw an assumed direction for each branch current.
At the principal node N, write KCL with each current as (voltage at one end − voltage at the other) ÷ R.
Solve for V_N.
Work out every current, voltage drop and power, then check the power balance.

Worked example
Two sources share a load. V_A = 24 V connects to node N through R_1 = 6\ \Omega. V_B = 12 V connects through R_3 = 4\ \Omega. A load R_2 = 12\ \Omega goes from N to ground. Find V_N and every current.


                  
                  Answer 
                  
                

KCL at N (currents from the sources in = current to ground out):
\frac{24 - V_N}{6} + \frac{12 - V_N}{4} = \frac{V_N}{12}
Multiply by 12: 2(24 - V_N) + 3(12 - V_N) = V_N → 84 = 6V_N → V_N = 14 V.
I_1 = (24 - 14)/6 = 1.67 A · I_3 = (12 - 14)/4 = -0.5 A · I_2 = 14/12 = 1.17 A
I_3 is negative: current flows into the 12 V source, which is being charged. KCL check: 1.67 - 0.5 = 1.17 ✓
Power: resistors 16.7 + 1.0 + 16.3 = 34 W. Sources: 24 \times 1.67 - 12 \times 0.5 = 40 - 6 = 34 W ✓


A source with negative power is absorbing energy, like a robot’s battery being charged by the main supply.
Common mistakes

Mixing directions: if every current is written as “flowing out of N”, then \sum = 0. If some are in and some out, then in = out. Pick one style and stick with it.
Forgetting to multiply through by a common denominator before rearranging.

Check yourself


                  
                  1. In the example, what would V_N be if the 12 V source were removed (its branch disconnected)?
                  
                

Now it’s a plain divider: 24 \times \dfrac{12}{6 + 12} = 16 V.

wm1ad/week-1/wheatstone-bridge-and-therm.title: Wheatstone bridge and thermistors
wm1ad/week-1/wheatstone-bridge-and-therm.content:
The idea
Sensors like thermistors, strain gauges and pressure sensors change their resistance by a tiny amount. A Wheatstone bridge turns that tiny change into a voltage you can measure. It’s two voltage dividers side by side, and you measure the difference between their middles.

The bridge
Each side is a voltage divider. Measured from B:
V_C = V\frac{R_2}{R_1 + R_2} \qquad V_D = V\frac{R_4}{R_3 + R_4} \qquad V_0 = V_C - V_D
It’s balanced (V_0 = 0) when the two dividers split the voltage the same way:
\frac{R_1}{R_2} = \frac{R_3}{R_4} \quad\Rightarrow\quad R_4 = \frac{R_2 R_3}{R_1}
So if three resistors are known, you can find the fourth by adjusting until the meter reads zero. Because it measures a difference, noise that affects both sides equally cancels out.
Thermistors
A thermistor is a resistor that changes a lot with temperature.

NTC (negative temperature coefficient): resistance falls as it gets hotter. The common type.
PTC (positive temperature coefficient): resistance rises. Often used as resettable fuses.

In robots they sense the temperature of battery packs, motors and power electronics, limit inrush current, and trigger thermal shutdowns.
The β model (temperatures in kelvin):
R(T) = R_0 \exp\!\left[B\left(\frac{1}{T} - \frac{1}{T_0}\right)\right]
R_0 is the resistance at T_0 (usually 25 °C = 298.15 K) and B is from the datasheet.
In a bridge with the thermistor in one arm and R_0 in the other three, it balances at 25 °C, and
V_0 = V_{ex}\left(\frac{R(T)}{R(T) + R_0} - \frac{1}{2}\right)
Near 25 °C the output changes by roughly \dfrac{V_{ex}}{4}\,\alpha per kelvin, where \alpha = -B/T_0^2.
Worked example
A 10 kΩ NTC thermistor (B = 3950 K) sits in a bridge with three 10 kΩ resistors, fed with 3.3 V. What’s the output at 0 °C?


                  
                  Answer 
                  
                

T = 273.15 K. \dfrac{1}{273.15} - \dfrac{1}{298.15} = 0.000307, × 3950 = 1.213
R = 10\,000\,e^{1.213} \approx 33.6 kΩ (colder, so higher resistance for an NTC)
V_0 = 3.3\left(\dfrac{33.6}{43.6} - 0.5\right) = 3.3 \times 0.271 =  +0.89 V
Sensitivity near 25 °C: \alpha = -3950/298.15^2 = -0.0444 K⁻¹, so about \frac{3.3}{4}(-0.0444) = -37 mV per °C.


Getting accurate readings





























Error sourceFixSelf-heating from the measuring currentKeep the excitation current smallResistor tolerance in the bridge0.1% resistorsADC offset and noiseAmplify and averageβ not exactCalibrate at two known temperaturesLong leads4-wire connection
Common mistakes

Using °C in the β equation. It must be kelvin.
Forgetting an NTC goes up when it’s cold.

Check yourself


                  
                  1. A bridge has R_1 = 1 kΩ, R_2 = 2.2 kΩ, R_3 = 4.7 kΩ. What R_4 balances it?
                  
                

R_4 = \dfrac{2.2 \times 4.7}{1} = 10.34 kΩ.

wm1ad/week-2/matrices-and-cramer's-rule.title: Matrices and Cramer's rule
wm1ad/week-2/matrices-and-cramer's-rule.content:
The idea
A circuit with three loops gives you three simultaneous equations. Writing them as a matrix keeps them tidy, and the determinant gives a mechanical way to solve them. You’ll use this in Mesh analysis, and it also turns up in WM1AC for vectors and robot kinematics.
Matrices
An m \times n matrix has m rows and n columns; a_{ij} is the element in row i, column j.

Add or subtract: same size only, element by element.
Multiply AB: the columns of A must equal the rows of B. (m\times n)(n\times p) \to (m\times p). Each element is a row of A dotted with a column of B.
\begin{bmatrix} 2 & 3 \\ 1 & 4 \end{bmatrix}\begin{bmatrix} 5 & 1 \\ 0 & 2 \end{bmatrix} = \begin{bmatrix} 10 & 8 \\ 5 & 9 \end{bmatrix}
Order matters: in general AB \neq BA.
There’s no division. "A \div B" means AB^{-1}, which only exists if \det B \neq 0.

Determinants
A single number from a square matrix. If it’s zero, the matrix has no inverse and the equations have no unique solution (the rows aren’t independent).
2×2:
\begin{vmatrix} a & b \\ c & d \end{vmatrix} = ad - bc
3×3: expand along any row or column. Each element times its minor (the 2×2 left when you cover its row and column), with signs from the chequerboard:
\begin{matrix} + & - & + \\ - & + & - \\ + & - & + \end{matrix}
Choose the row or column with the most zeros to save work.
2×2 inverse: swap the main diagonal, negate the other two, divide by the determinant:
\begin{bmatrix} a & b \\ c & d \end{bmatrix}^{-1} = \frac{1}{ad - bc}\begin{bmatrix} d & -b \\ -c & a \end{bmatrix}
Cramer’s rule
For equations A\mathbf{x} = \mathbf{b}:

Find \Delta = \det A.
For each unknown, replace its column of A with \mathbf b and take that determinant, \Delta_k.
x_k = \Delta_k / \Delta.
Substitute back to check.

Worked example
Find \det\begin{bmatrix} 3 & 1 & 2 \\ 0 & 4 & 1 \\ 2 & -1 & 3 \end{bmatrix}, then solve 2x + 3y = 13, x - y = -1 with Cramer’s rule.


                  
                  Answer 
                  
                

Expand along column 1 (it has a zero): 3\begin{vmatrix} 4 & 1 \\ -1 & 3 \end{vmatrix} - 0 + 2\begin{vmatrix} 1 & 2 \\ 4 & 1 \end{vmatrix} = 3(13) + 2(1 - 8) = 39 - 14 =  25
\Delta = \begin{vmatrix} 2 & 3 \\ 1 & -1 \end{vmatrix} = -2 - 3 = -5
\Delta_x = \begin{vmatrix} 13 & 3 \\ -1 & -1 \end{vmatrix} = -13 + 3 = -10 → x = 2
\Delta_y = \begin{vmatrix} 2 & 13 \\ 1 & -1 \end{vmatrix} = -2 - 13 = -15 → y = 3
Check: 2(2) + 3(3) = 13 ✓, 2 - 3 = -1 ✓


On the calculator and in MATLAB

Scientific calculators (e.g. Casio fx-991) have a Matrix mode for determinants and an Equation / Simul mode that solves 3×3 systems directly. Use Cramer when you need to show working.
MATLAB: A = [2, 3; 1, -1] (commas separate columns, semicolons rows), det(A), and x = A\b with b = [13; -1]. b must be a column, so use ;.

Common mistakes

Forgetting the minus sign in the middle of the + - + pattern.
Multiplying matrices element by element.
Putting the constants in the wrong column for \Delta_k.

Check yourself


                  
                  1. Inverse of \begin{bmatrix} 4 & 2 \\ 3 & 5 \end{bmatrix}?
                  
                

\Delta = 20 - 6 = 14, so \dfrac{1}{14}\begin{bmatrix} 5 & -2 \\ -3 & 4 \end{bmatrix}.




                  
                  2. Why does \begin{bmatrix} 1 & 2 \\ 2 & 4 \end{bmatrix} have no inverse?
                  
                

Its determinant is 4 - 4 = 0: the second row is just twice the first.

wm1ad/week-2/mesh-analysis.title: Mesh analysis
wm1ad/week-2/mesh-analysis.content:
The idea
Give every loop (“mesh”) in the circuit its own current going round clockwise. Write KVL for each loop and you get one equation per mesh, which fit neatly into a matrix. Solve it and you have every current in the circuit at once.

A typical robot example: the main supply (V_1) and a backup battery (V_2) both feed a motor drive. Simplified, that’s two sources and five resistors in three meshes.
Building the matrix by inspection
\begin{bmatrix} R_1 + R_2 & -R_2 & 0 \\ -R_2 & R_2 + R_3 + R_4 & -R_4 \\ 0 & -R_4 & R_4 + R_5 \end{bmatrix}\begin{bmatrix} I_1 \\ I_2 \\ I_3 \end{bmatrix} = \begin{bmatrix} V_1 \\ 0 \\ V_2 \end{bmatrix}

Diagonal: the total resistance round that mesh.
Off-diagonal: minus the resistance shared by the two meshes, or 0 if they share nothing. So the matrix is always symmetric.
Right-hand side: the source voltage driving each mesh, or 0.

Then:

Solve for the mesh currents (Cramer, calculator or MATLAB).
An outer branch carries its own mesh current.
A shared branch carries the difference of the two mesh currents. A negative answer means it flows the other way.
Power balance: \sum I^2R = \sum VI.

Worked example
V_1 = 24 V, V_2 = 12 V, R_1 = 4, R_2 = 6, R_3 = 3, R_4 = 8, R_5 = 2\ \Omega. Find every branch current and check the power balance.


                  
                  Answer 
                  
                

\begin{bmatrix} 10 & -6 & 0 \\ -6 & 17 & -8 \\ 0 & -8 & 10 \end{bmatrix}\begin{bmatrix} I_1 \\ I_2 \\ I_3 \end{bmatrix} = \begin{bmatrix} 24 \\ 0 \\ 12 \end{bmatrix} \qquad \Delta = 700
\Delta_1 = 3120, \Delta_2 = 2400, \Delta_3 = 2760, so I_1 = 4.457 A, I_2 = 3.429 A, I_3 = 3.943 A.
Branches: I_{R1} = 4.457, I_{R3} = 3.429, I_{R5} = 3.943 A.
Shared: I_{R2} = I_1 - I_2 = 1.029 A, I_{R4} = I_2 - I_3 = -0.514 A (flows opposite to I_2‘s direction).
Resistors: 79.46 + 6.35 + 35.27 + 2.12 + 31.09 = 154.3 W
Sources: 24 \times 4.457 + 12 \times 3.943 = 107.0 + 47.3 = 154.3 W ✓


Common mistakes

Positive off-diagonal terms. Shared resistances are always negative in this setup.
Forgetting a resistor in a diagonal term: go all the way round the mesh.
Reading a shared branch’s current as one mesh current instead of the difference.

Check yourself


                  
                  1. Write the matrix for R_1 = 5, R_2 = 3, R_3 = 2, R_4 = 4, R_5 = 7\ \Omega, V_1 = 24 V, V_2 = 12 V.
                  
                

\begin{bmatrix} 8 & -3 & 0 \\ -3 & 9 & -4 \\ 0 & -4 & 11 \end{bmatrix}\begin{bmatrix} I_1 \\ I_2 \\ I_3 \end{bmatrix} = \begin{bmatrix} 24 \\ 0 \\ 12 \end{bmatrix}, giving I_1 = 3.78, I_2 = 2.08, I_3 = 1.85 A.

wm1ad/week-2/rc-transients.title: RC transients
wm1ad/week-2/rc-transients.content:
The idea
A capacitor can’t change its voltage instantly; it has to fill with charge through whatever resistance is in the way. So when you switch on an RC circuit, the voltage climbs along a curve instead of jumping. In a robot this happens every time the power supply charges the capacitor bank (DC link) in front of a motor drive through the cable resistance.

The time constant
\tau = RC \quad \text{(seconds)}





















Time1τ2τ3τ4τ5τCharged to63.2%86.5%95.0%98.2%99.3%
After 5τ, call it fully charged (or discharged).
Deriving the curves
This is your first engineering ODE (ordinary differential equation): its answer is a function of time, not a number.

Component laws: u_R = iR and i = C\dfrac{du_C}{dt} (current is the rate of change of the capacitor’s charge).
KVL round the loop while charging from V: V = u_R + u_C = RC\dfrac{du_C}{dt} + u_C.
Separate the variables and integrate from u_C = 0 at t = 0:

u_C(t) = V\left(1 - e^{-t/\tau}\right) \qquad i(t) = \frac{V}{R}e^{-t/\tau}
Discharging from V_0 (no source, so RC\,\dfrac{du_C}{dt} + u_C = 0):
u_C(t) = V_0\,e^{-t/\tau} \qquad i(t) = -\frac{V_0}{R}e^{-t/\tau}
The minus sign means the current now flows the other way.
Energy

A charged capacitor holds E = \tfrac12 CV^2.
Charging it through a resistor always wastes exactly as much energy as it stores, whatever R is. Half the energy from the source becomes heat.

Capacitors combine the opposite way to resistors

Parallel: C = C_1 + C_2, same voltage rating. Two 500 µF, 24 V capacitors → 1000 µF, 24 V.
Series: \dfrac{1}{C} = \dfrac{1}{C_1} + \dfrac{1}{C_2}, voltage ratings add. Two 500 µF, 24 V in series → 250 µF, 48 V.

Worked example
A 12 V supply charges a 100 µF capacitor through 47 kΩ. Find τ, the voltage after 4.7 s and after 10 s, the time to reach 9 V, and the starting current.


                  
                  Answer 
                  
                

\tau = 47\,000 \times 100\times10^{-6} = 4.7 s
At 4.7 s (1τ): 12(1 - e^{-1}) = 7.59 V
At 10 s: 12(1 - e^{-10/4.7}) = 12(1 - 0.119) = 10.57 V
To 9 V: 9 = 12(1 - e^{-t/4.7}) → e^{-t/4.7} = 0.25 → t = 4.7\ln 4 = 6.52 s
i(0) = 12/47\,000 = 0.255 mA. Stored when full: \tfrac12 \times 100\times10^{-6} \times 12^2 = 7.2 mJ.


Common mistakes

Using µF without the 10^{-6}.
Using the charging equation for a discharge.
Taking a log of the wrong side: isolate e^{-t/\tau} first, then take ln of both sides.

Check yourself


                  
                  1. A 10 Ω, 220 µF circuit. How long until it's fully charged? 
                  
                

\tau = 2.2 ms, so about 5\tau = 11 ms.




                  
                  2. Why is it said a capacitor "looks like a short circuit" at switch-on? 
                  
                

At t = 0 it has no voltage across it, so the current is the full V/R, as if the capacitor were a wire.

wm1ad/week-3/ac-values.title: AC values
wm1ad/week-3/ac-values.content:
The idea
Mains electricity is a sine wave: it pushes current one way, then the other, 50 times a second in the UK. The “230 V” printed on everything isn’t the top of that wave. It’s the RMS value, the steady DC voltage that would heat a kettle by the same amount. The wave itself peaks at 325 V, and any part connected to mains has to survive that peak.

The three numbers





























SymbolNameWhat it isUK mainsV_{pk}PeakThe top of the wave325 VV_{RMS}RMSThe heating-equivalent value. What meters and labels quote230 VV_{avg}AverageThe mean height of one hump of the wave207 V

























ConvertMultiply byRMS → peak\sqrt2 \approx 1.41Peak → RMS1/\sqrt2 \approx 0.707Peak → average2/\pi \approx 0.637RMS → average0.9
Where the numbers come from
RMS means root of the mean of the square. We square because heating power goes as V^2.

The wave is V = V_{pk}\sin\theta, so V^2 = V_{pk}^2\sin^2\theta.
Over a whole cycle, \sin^2\theta averages to exactly \tfrac12.
So the mean of the square is \tfrac12 V_{pk}^2, and its root is

V_{RMS} = \frac{V_{pk}}{\sqrt2} \quad\Rightarrow\quad V_{pk} = \sqrt2 \times 230 = 325.3\ \text{V}
Average of one hump = area ÷ width. The area under \sin\theta from 0 to \pi is exactly 2, and the width is \pi:
V_{avg} = \frac{2}{\pi}V_{pk} = 0.637\,V_{pk} \qquad \frac{V_{avg}}{V_{RMS}} = \frac{0.637}{0.707} = 0.9
The same ratios apply to current through a resistive load, so I_{avg} = 0.9\,I_{RMS}. You’ll need that for bridge losses.
Worked example
A robot’s charger is plugged into a 110 V RMS (US) supply. What peak voltage must its rectifier survive, and what’s the average of each hump?


                  
                  Answer 
                  
                

V_{pk} = 1.41 \times 110 = 155.6 V. V_{avg} = 0.637 \times 155.6 = 99.1 V (or 0.9 \times 110 = 99 V).
A diode rated V_{RRM} = 400 V would be fine. At 230 V you’d want 600–800 V.


Common mistakes

Using 230 V where the question needs the peak. Capacitors charge to the peak, and diodes must block the peak.
Using RMS current for a diode’s loss. Diodes use average current (see Bridge rectifiers).
Trusting a cheap multimeter on PWM. Ordinary meters only read RMS correctly for a clean 50 Hz sine. Use a true-RMS meter or a scope.

Check yourself


                  
                  1. A sine wave has a peak-to-peak voltage of 40 V. What's its RMS value? 
                  
                

Peak = 20 V, so RMS = 0.707 × 20 = 14.1 V.




                  
                  2. Why is RMS defined with a square? 
                  
                

Because heating power in a resistor is V^2/R. Averaging V^2 gives a voltage that delivers the same power as DC.

wm1ad/week-3/bridge-rectifiers.title: Bridge rectifiers
wm1ad/week-3/bridge-rectifiers.content:
The idea
A diode is a one-way valve for current. In the symbol, current can only flow the way the triangle points, and getting through costs a small, roughly fixed voltage, the forward voltage V_F \approx 1 V. Backwards, it blocks, up to its limit V_{RRM}.
One diode on its own (a half-wave rectifier) lets the positive half of the AC through and throws the negative half away. A full bridge uses four diodes arranged in a diamond so that both halves come out positive.
How the bridge works
Name the four corners: A and B connect to the AC, + and − connect to the load.

























DiodeAllows currentD1A → +D2B → +D3− → AD4− → B
Two arrows point into +, two point out of −. So whatever the AC does, current can only arrive at + and leave from −. It always goes through the load from + to −.

Positive half (A pushes): A → D1 → + → load → − → D4 → B. D2 and D3 would need current to flow against their arrows, so they block.

Negative half (B pushes): B → D2 → + → load → − → D3 → A. Same direction through the load.


                  
                  The two things to remember 
                  
                


Current always passes through exactly two diodes. So the output peak is V_{pk} - 2V_F, and two diodes are always making heat.
The output is a row of positive humps, two per AC cycle: 100 per second at 50 Hz.



A three-phase bridge (6 diodes) on a three-phase supply gives six overlapping humps per cycle, which is nearly flat DC. That’s what big industrial kit uses.
Smoothing with a capacitor
The humps still drop to 0 V between peaks. A capacitor across the output works like a water tank: it fills at each peak, and the load drains it a little until the next hump refills it. The dip is the ripple, \Delta V.

Deriving the ripple:

Refills happen 100 times a second, so the gap is \Delta t = \dfrac{1}{2F_{grid}} = 10 ms.
In that gap the load takes charge \Delta Q = I\,\Delta t (current is charge per second).
For a capacitor Q = CV, so the voltage drops by \Delta V = \Delta Q / C.

\boxed{\Delta V = \frac{I}{2\,F_{grid}\,C}}
The capacitor charges to the top of each hump, minus the two diode drops:
V_{C,max} = V_{pk} - 2V_F
Heat in the bridge

Power = voltage × current. A conducting diode has a fixed V_F across it, so P = V_F \times i at every instant.
Averaged over time, V_F is constant, so P = V_F \times I_{avg}. Diodes use average current, unlike resistors and MOSFETs, which use I^2R with RMS.
Two diodes are always on, so P = 2\,V_F\,I_{avg}.
You’re usually given RMS, and for these humps I_{avg} = 0.9\,I_{RMS} (see AC values).

\boxed{P_{D(FB)} = 2 \times 0.9 \times V_F\,I_{D,RMS} = 1.8\,V_F\,I_{D,RMS}}
Choosing a bridge from its datasheet

























CheckRuleWhyI_{F(AV)}Above your current, with margin (~50%)It sets how much average current it can carry without overheatingV_{RRM}Above the peak, 325 V on UK mains, with marginWhen a diode is off, it has to block the full peakV_FLower is betterLess heat, slightly higher output
Worked example
A robot charger uses a GBPC12 bridge (V_F = 1.1 V, I_{F(AV)} = 12 A, V_{RRM} = 800 V) on 230 V mains. It draws 2 A RMS and has a 4700 µF smoothing capacitor. Find the bridge’s heat, the capacitor’s peak voltage and the ripple. Is the bridge suitable?


                  
                  Answer 
                  
                

P_{D(FB)} = 1.8 \times 1.1 \times 2 = 3.96 W
V_{C,max} = 325.3 - 2(1.1) = 323.1 V
\Delta V = \dfrac{2}{2 \times 50 \times 4700\times10^{-6}} = \dfrac{2}{0.47} = 4.26 V
Suitable: 12 A ≫ 2 A, and 800 V > 325 V.


Common mistakes

Forgetting the two diode drops: it’s V_{pk} - 2V_F, not - V_F.
Forgetting µF is \times10^{-6}. 4700 µF = 0.0047 F.
Using 50 instead of 2 \times 50 in the ripple formula. A full bridge refills twice per cycle.
Checking V_{RRM} against 230 V instead of the 325 V peak.

Check yourself


                  
                  1. In the positive half, why doesn't current go A → D3? 
                  
                

D3 only allows − → A. Going A → − would be against its arrow, so it blocks.




                  
                  2. You double C. What happens to the ripple? 
                  
                

It halves, because \Delta V \propto 1/C.




                  
                  3. A bridge with V_F = 0.9 V carries 3 A RMS. How much heat does it make?
                  
                

1.8 \times 0.9 \times 3 = 4.86 W.

wm1ad/week-3/dc-dc-converters.title: DC-DC converters
wm1ad/week-3/dc-dc-converters.content:
The idea
A battery gives one voltage, but a robot needs several: one for the motors, one for the logic, one for the sensors. A DC-DC converter chops the input with a MOSFET (PWM), then smooths the result with an inductor (which stores energy in its current) and a capacitor (which stores energy in its voltage). The duty cycle D sets the output.
Buck (step-down)


Switch on: the battery drives current through L into the load. L stores energy.
Switch off: L keeps the current flowing (inductors resist sudden changes in current), and the diode completes the loop. This is called freewheeling.

\boxed{V_{out} = D\,V_{in}}
Boost (step-up)


Switch on: L is connected straight across the battery and charges up. The capacitor feeds the load.
Switch off: the battery and L push together through the diode, so the output rises above V_{in}.

\boxed{V_{out} = \frac{V_{in}}{1-D}}
Deriving both: volt-second balance
In steady state, an inductor’s average voltage over one cycle must be zero. If it weren’t, its current would keep growing every cycle. So (voltage × time while on) + (voltage × time while off) = 0.
Buck. On for DT: the inductor sits between V_{in} and V_{out}, so V_L = V_{in} - V_{out}. Off for (1-D)T: the diode connects it to ground, so V_L = -V_{out}.
(V_{in} - V_{out})\,D = V_{out}\,(1-D) \;\Rightarrow\; V_{out} = D\,V_{in}
Boost. On: V_L = V_{in}. Off: V_L = V_{in} - V_{out}, which is negative.
V_{in}D + (V_{in} - V_{out})(1-D) = 0 \;\Rightarrow\; V_{out} = \frac{V_{in}}{1-D}
Sizing the buck’s L and C
Inductor: V = L\,\dfrac{\Delta I}{\Delta t}. While off, V_L = V_{out} for a time (1-D)/F_{SW}, and the current changes by the ripple \Delta I_L:
\boxed{L = \frac{V_{out}(1-D)}{F_{SW}\,\Delta I_L}}
Capacitor: it absorbs the inductor’s triangle-shaped ripple current:
\boxed{C_{out} \ge \frac{\Delta I_L}{8\,F_{SW}\,\Delta V_{out}}}
Higher frequency means a smaller L and C, which is why modern converters are tiny. The trade-off is more switching loss.
Worked example
Step a 48 V robot battery down to 24 V at 5 A, switching at 100 kHz, with 10% ripple on both current and voltage. Find D, L and C.


                  
                  Answer 
                  
                

D = 24/48 = 0.5. \Delta I_L = 0.1 \times 5 = 0.5 A. \Delta V = 0.1 \times 24 = 2.4 V.
L = \dfrac{24 \times 0.5}{100\,000 \times 0.5} = 240\ \muH
C \ge \dfrac{0.5}{8 \times 100\,000 \times 2.4} = 0.26\ \muF


Isolated or not?








































Transformer-less (buck, boost)Transformer-based (isolated)HowSwitch, inductor, capacitorDC → high-frequency AC → transformer → rectified back to DCGalvanic isolationNo: a fault passes to the loadYes: protects the user and loadEfficiency90–98%80–95%Size and costSmall, cheapBulkier, costs moreVoltage ratioLow to moderateExtreme step-up or step-downOutputsOneOne or several
Buck-boost converters can go either way, which is useful when a battery sags below the output as it drains. Synchronous versions replace the diode with a second MOSFET to cut loss.
Check yourself


                  
                  1. A boost converter takes 12 V and must output 36 V. What duty cycle? 
                  
                

36 = 12/(1-D) → 1 - D = 1/3 → D = 0.667.




                  
                  2. In the buck L formula, which voltage goes on top, V_{in} or V_{out}?
                  
                

V_{out}. During the off-time, the inductor has V_{out} across it.

wm1ad/week-3/mosfet-power-loss.title: MOSFET power loss
wm1ad/week-3/mosfet-power-loss.content:
The idea
A MOSFET wastes power in two separate ways:

Conduction loss: while it’s fully on, current flows through its small on-resistance R_{DS(on)}.
Switching loss: while it’s changing state, for a few nanoseconds there’s a large voltage across it and a large current through it at the same time. This happens twice per cycle, so it grows with the switching frequency.


When it’s off there’s full voltage but no current, so no loss. When it’s on there’s full current but only a tiny voltage (I \times R_{DS(on)}), so a small loss. The red spikes are where both are large together.
Conduction loss
Fully on, the MOSFET is just a resistor of value R_{DS(on)}, so
\boxed{P_{cond} = R_{DS(on)}\,I_D^2}
Because of the square, doubling the current quadruples this loss. That’s why high-power systems use higher voltages (less current for the same power), and why MOSFETs are often put in parallel to share current.
Switching loss, derived

During turn-on, the current first rises from 0 to I_D while the voltage is still V_{DD}. Then the voltage falls to almost 0 while the current stays at I_D.
In each part, the power V \times I ramps between 0 and V_{DD}I_D, which makes a triangle on a power–time graph.
Energy is the area under the power graph. A triangle’s area is ½ × height × width, so over the whole switching time t:

E = \tfrac12\,V_{DD}\,I_D\,t

The datasheet splits the switching time into two parts each way:

E_{ON} = \frac{V_{DD} I_D}{2}\,\big(t_{d(on)} + t_r\big) \qquad E_{OFF} = \frac{V_{DD} I_D}{2}\,\big(t_{d(off)} + t_f\big)

There’s one turn-on and one turn-off per cycle, F_{SW} times a second, and energy per second is power:

\boxed{P_{SW} = (E_{ON} + E_{OFF})\,F_{SW}} \qquad \boxed{P_{MOSFET} = P_{cond} + P_{SW}}
(The full formula has an extra Q_{rr}V_{DD} term for diode recovery charge. It’s usually ignored at this level.)
Worked example
An IRFP140 (R_{DS(on)} = 0.077 Ω; t_{d(on)} = 11, t_r = 44, t_{d(off)} = 53, t_f = 43 ns) switches a 36 V motor supply at 8 A. Find the total loss at 20 kHz, then at 150 kHz.


                  
                  Answer 
                  
                

P_{cond} = 0.077 \times 8^2 = 0.077 \times 64 = 4.93 W
\dfrac{V_{DD}I_D}{2} = \dfrac{36 \times 8}{2} = 144
E_{ON} = 144 \times (11+44)\times10^{-9} = 144 \times 55\times10^{-9} = 7.92\ \muJ
E_{OFF} = 144 \times (53+43)\times10^{-9} = 144 \times 96\times10^{-9} = 13.82\ \muJ
At 20 kHz: P_{SW} = 21.74\times10^{-6} \times 20\,000 = 0.43 W, so P_{MOSFET} = 5.36 W (conduction dominates).
At 150 kHz: P_{SW} = 21.74\times10^{-6} \times 150\,000 = 3.26 W, so P_{MOSFET} = 8.19 W. Switching loss has caught up.


What drives each loss



































ChangeP_{cond}P_{SW}Double the current×4×2Double the voltageno change×2Double the frequencyno change×2Pick a part with half the R_{DS(on)}×½no changePick a faster part (shorter times)no changesmaller
Common mistakes

Squaring the wrong thing. Square the current only: 10^2 = 100, not 100^2.
Forgetting nanoseconds. ns = \times10^{-9}.
Adding the wrong pair of times. On = t_{d(on)} + t_r, off = t_{d(off)} + t_f.
kHz. 13 kHz = 13 000 Hz.
Mixing numbers from two questions. Sanity check: the loss can never exceed V_{DD} \times I_D.

Check yourself


                  
                  1. An IRFP250 ( R_{DS(on)} = 0.075 Ω; 14 + 43 ns on, 41 + 33 ns off) runs at 24 V, 10 A, 13 kHz. Total loss?
                  
                

P_{cond} = 0.075 \times 100 = 7.5 W. E_{ON} = 120 \times 57\times10^{-9} = 6.84\ \muJ, E_{OFF} = 120 \times 74\times10^{-9} = 8.88\ \muJ. P_{SW} = 15.72\times10^{-6} \times 13\,000 = 0.20 W. Total ≈ 7.7 W.




                  
                  2. Why is switching loss more important in DC-DC converters than in a simple motor PWM? 
                  
                

Converters run at 100+ kHz to keep the inductor and capacitor small, and switching loss scales with frequency.


Next: what to do with all that heat, in Thermal design and heatsinks.

wm1ad/week-3/motor-drives.title: Motor drives
wm1ad/week-3/motor-drives.content:
The idea
The last link in the chain is a set of switches arranged so the motor gets the right voltage, polarity and timing. PWM sets the speed. The arrangement of switches sets the direction, and for brushless motors, which coil is energised.
Brushed DC: the H-bridge
One MOSFET with PWM (a single-switch chopper) controls speed, but only in one direction. To reverse the motor you need to flip the polarity across it. Four switches in an H do that:



























Switches onResultS1 + S4Forward: current left → right through the motorS2 + S3Reverse: current right → leftS3 + S4Brake: the motor’s terminals are shorted, so its own back-EMF slows it fastS1 + S3 or S2 + S4Never. This connects +V straight to 0 V through two switches (shoot-through), which destroys them. Drivers add dead time to prevent it
The driver must also carry the motor’s continuous current, and should limit it so a stalled motor doesn’t overheat.
Brushless (BLDC, PMSM): the three-phase inverter
Three half-bridges, one per motor phase (U, V, W), six switches in total. Switching them in sequence makes a rotating magnetic field that drags the magnet rotor round. With no brushes, there’s less wear and higher efficiency.
P_{in,motor} = \sqrt3\,V_L\,I_{phase,RMS}\cos\varphi \qquad V_L = \frac{V_{DC}}{\sqrt2}
I_{phase,RMS} = \frac{P_{out}}{\sqrt3\,V_L\cos\varphi\,\eta} \qquad I_{D,RMS} = \frac{I_{phase,RMS}}{\sqrt2}

\cos\varphi is the power factor, typically 0.92–1. \eta is the efficiency, typically 90–95%.
The last formula has a \sqrt2 because each transistor carries its phase’s current only half the time, and RMS scales with the square root of the on-time (\sqrt{1/2} = 1/\sqrt2). That I_{D,RMS} is what goes into the MOSFET power loss calculation.

Worked example
A 500 W brushless motor runs from a 48 V battery, with \cos\varphi = 0.95 and \eta = 0.92. Find the phase current and the current through each transistor.


                  
                  Answer 
                  
                

V_L = 48/\sqrt2 = 33.9 V
I_{phase} = \dfrac{500}{1.732 \times 33.9 \times 0.95 \times 0.92} = \dfrac{500}{51.4} = 9.73 A
I_{D,RMS} = 9.73/1.414 = 6.88 A per transistor


Stepper motors




















TypeCoilsDriverBipolarTwo separate coilsTwo H-bridges, to reverse the current in each coilUnipolarCentre-tapped coilsSimple low-side switches that pull each half-coil to ground in turn
Both use PWM current chopping: the driver measures the coil current and switches off the instant it reaches the rated limit.
Check yourself


                  
                  1. Which pair of switches in an H-bridge must never be on together, and why? 
                  
                

Two on the same side (S1 + S3, or S2 + S4). They short the supply to ground.




                  
                  2. How many H-bridges does a bipolar stepper need? 
                  
                

Two, one per coil.

wm1ad/week-3/pwm.title: PWM
wm1ad/week-3/pwm.content:
The idea
A MOSFET is either fully on or fully off. To give a motor some of the power, switch it on for part of each cycle, thousands of times a second. The motor is far too slow to notice the flicker, so it responds to the average voltage. This is pulse width modulation (PWM).
The definitions





















SymbolMeaningTPeriod: the time for one on-plus-off cycle, T = t_{on} + t_{off}FFrequency: cycles per second, F = 1/TDDuty cycle: fraction of the time it’s on, D = t_{on}/T, from 0 to 1
\boxed{V_{avg} = D \times V_{DD}}
Why: for a fraction D of the time the motor sees V_{DD}, and for the rest it sees 0 V. The average is D \times V_{DD} + (1-D)\times 0.
Worked example
A 24 V battery drives a motor with PWM at 20 kHz and 30% duty. Find T, t_{on} and the average voltage.


                  
                  Answer 
                  
                

T = 1/20\,000 = 50 µs. t_{on} = 0.3 \times 50 = 15 µs, so t_{off} = 35 µs.
V_{avg} = 0.3 \times 24 = 7.2 V.


Why the frequency matters

Too low (under ~1 kHz) and you can hear the motor whine, and the current ripples a lot.
Higher frequencies give smoother current and smaller converter parts, but every switch costs energy, so switching loss rises with frequency.

Check yourself


                  
                  1. What duty cycle gives 9 V from a 12 V supply? 
                  
                

D = 9/12 = 0.75, so 75%.

wm1ad/week-3/power-switches.title: Power switches
wm1ad/week-3/power-switches.content:
The idea
To control a motor you need a switch that turns power on and off, often thousands of times a second. A relay does it mechanically. Transistors do it electronically: a small control signal on one leg lets a large current flow through the other two. The key difference between transistor types is what the control signal is, a current or a voltage.
The transistors
BJT (bipolar junction transistor): current-controlled. Legs: base (B), collector (C), emitter (E). A small base current I_B lets a large collector current flow, roughly I_C = \beta I_B. The drawback is that the base needs current all the time it’s on, which wastes power. NPN and PNP types are biased opposite ways round.
MOSFET: voltage-controlled. Legs: gate (G), drain (D), source (S). The gate is insulated from the channel by a thin layer of silicon dioxide, so almost no gate current flows. Raise the gate–source voltage V_{GS} above the threshold V_{GS(th)} and current flows drain → source. Fully on, it behaves like a small resistor, R_{DS(on)}.
IGBT (insulated gate bipolar transistor): a hybrid. It has a MOSFET’s insulated, voltage-driven gate and a BJT’s high-power output stage. Same structure as a MOSFET plus an extra P layer.
Comparison















































SwitchControlled byStrengthsWeaknessesTypical useRelayCoil current moves a contactCheap, takes surges, true isolation, cool, several polesSlow, wears out, sparks, vibration-sensitiveOccasional mains switchingSSR (solid-state relay)Small input signalLong life, fast, silent, no arcing, tiny control powerGets hot, costs more, leaks a little current, surge-sensitiveFrequent switching, heatersBJTBase currentSimple, cheapNeeds continuous drive current, slowerSmall signalsMOSFETGate voltageVery fast, easy to driveR_{DS(on)} rises in high-voltage partsRobots and motor drives, below ~700 VIGBTGate voltageHigh voltage and currentSlower switchingAbove ~1000 V: trains, grid, large inverters


                  
                  Rule of thumb 
                  
                

MOSFET below about 700 V, IGBT above about 1000 V. In between, pick whichever best fits the size, efficiency and cost.


Reading a MOSFET datasheet






















































ValueSectionWhat it tells youIRFP140IRFP250V_{DSS}Absolute maxMost voltage it can block when off100 V200 VI_DAbsolute maxMost continuous current (falls when hot)31 A30 AR_{DS(on)}StaticResistance when fully on, for conduction loss0.077 Ω0.075 Ωt_{d(on)}, t_rDynamicTurn-on delay and rise time11, 44 ns14, 43 nst_{d(off)}, t_fDynamicTurn-off delay and fall time53, 43 ns41, 33 nsR_{thJC}, R_{thCS}, R_{thJA}ThermalFor heatsink sizing0.83, 0.24, 40 °C/W0.7, 0.24, 40 °C/W
Check yourself


                  
                  1. Why does a MOSFET need almost no drive power once it's on? 
                  
                

Its gate is insulated, so it only needs a voltage, with no continuous current. A BJT’s base needs current the whole time.




                  
                  2. You need to switch 48 V at 20 A, 20 000 times a second. Relay, BJT, MOSFET or IGBT? 
                  
                

A MOSFET: low voltage, fast switching. A relay is far too slow, and an IGBT is aimed at much higher voltages.

wm1ad/week-3/thermal-design-and-heatsink.title: Thermal design and heatsinks
wm1ad/week-3/thermal-design-and-heatsink.content:
The idea
Every watt a component loses becomes heat inside its silicon junction. That heat has to flow out through the case, into a heatsink, then into the air. Each step resists the flow, so the junction ends up hotter than the air. Treat it exactly like Ohm’s law: heat flow behaves like current, temperature like voltage, and thermal resistance like resistance.






























ElectricalThermalCurrent I (A)Heat flow P (W)Voltage difference (V)Temperature difference \Delta T (°C)Resistance R (Ω)Thermal resistance R_{th} (°C/W)V = IR\Delta T = P\,R_{th}Series resistors addR_{th1} + R_{th2} + R_{th3}



































ResistanceFromToWhere you get itR_{th1} (R_{thJC})junctioncaseDatasheetR_{th2} (R_{thCS})caseheatsinkDatasheet (greased), more with an insulating padR_{th3}heatsinkairYou choose it by picking a heatsinkR_{thJA}junctionair, with no heatsinkDatasheet
Junction temperature
The same heat P flows through every step, like current through series resistors. Start from the air, which you know, and climb:
T_{hs} = T_{amb} + P R_{th3} \;\rightarrow\; T_C = T_{hs} + P R_{th2} \;\rightarrow\; T_J = T_C + P R_{th1}
\boxed{T_J = T_{amb} + P\,(R_{th1} + R_{th2} + R_{th3})}
With no heatsink, use the single datasheet value instead: T_J = T_{amb} + P\,R_{thJA}.
The limits:

Silicon’s absolute maximum is 175 °C. Design for 100–120 °C, and never above 120 °C.
Safety margin: \text{margin} = 100 - \dfrac{T_J}{175}\times100, aiming for at least 30%. 120 °C gives 31.4%.

Sizing a heatsink
Rearrange for the one resistance you choose:
\boxed{R_{th3} = \frac{T_J - T_{amb}}{P} - (R_{th1} + R_{th2})}
Put in your target T_J, and the answer is the largest R_{th3} you can get away with. Pick a heatsink at or below it. Lower °C/W means a bigger heatsink.


                  
                  A negative answer 
                  
                

If R_{th3} comes out negative, even a perfect heatsink (R_{th3} = 0) can’t keep the part cool, because R_{th1} + R_{th2} alone already make it too hot. The fixes:

a better interface (thermal grease, about 0.24 °C/W, instead of an insulating pad)
less loss: lower switching frequency, a part with lower R_{DS(on)}, or MOSFETs in parallel
a lower ambient temperature, or forced-air or liquid cooling



Worked example
The IRFP140 from MOSFET power loss dissipates 5.36 W in a robot whose electronics bay reaches 35 °C. Datasheet: R_{thJC} = 0.83, R_{thCS} = 0.24 (greased), R_{thJA} = 40 °C/W.

Can it run without a heatsink?
What heatsink keeps T_J at 100 °C?
You fit an 8 °C/W heatsink. What are T_J and the margin?



                  
                  Answer 
                  
                


T_J = 35 + 5.36 \times 40 = 249 °C. No. It’s far over 175 °C.
R_{th3} = \dfrac{100 - 35}{5.36} - (0.83 + 0.24) = 12.13 - 1.07 = 11.1 °C/W. Any heatsink at or below 11 °C/W works.
T_J = 35 + 5.36 \times (0.83 + 0.24 + 8) = 35 + 48.6 = 83.6 °C. Margin = 100 - \dfrac{83.6}{175}\times100 = 52\% ✓



Common mistakes

Adding the thermal resistances but forgetting to add T_{amb} at the end.
Reading “lower R_{th3}” as “smaller heatsink”. It’s the opposite.
Mixing R_{thJA} (no heatsink) with the three-step chain. Use one or the other.

Check yourself


                  
                  1. 40 W, R_{th1} = 0.7, R_{th2} = 2.0 (insulating pad), 50 °C ambient, target 120 °C. What heatsink?
                  
                

R_{th3} = 70/40 - 2.7 = 1.75 - 2.7 = -0.95 °C/W. Negative, so it’s impossible. Swap the pad for grease: 1.75 - 0.94 = 0.81 °C/W, which is a big but possible heatsink.




                  
                  2. P = 10 W, T_{amb} = 60 °C, R_{th} = 0.5, 1, 2 °C/W. Find T_{hs}, T_C and T_J.
                  
                

T_{hs} = 60 + 20 = 80 °C, T_C = 80 + 10 = 90 °C, T_J = 90 + 5 = 95 °C.

course.title: The course
course.content:
Overview
Robotics Engineering with Artificial Intelligence (BEng) at WMG, University of Warwick is a three-year degree that combines mechanical, electrical and software engineering with AI, aimed at designing and building robotic systems. 2026–27 is the first year it has run. WMG plans to seek IET accreditation for it (see accreditation and AHEP), and there’s an optional year in industry or research.
How Year 1 is structured
Year 1 is 120 credits, all core. You have to pass every module (pass mark 40%), but Year 1 marks don’t count towards your final degree classification. Years 2 and 3 count 30% and 70%.
Instead of running every module all year, the course is taught in blocks: three modules at a time, each with its own lectures, seminars and labs.





























BlockWhenModulesCredits1Oct – early DecWM1AD Electrical Power and Motors · WM1AC Mechanisms and Machines · WM199 Developing an Engineering Mindset15 each2Dec – early MarWM1AA Rapid Prototyping · WM1AE Programmable Electronics · WM1AF Engineering Systems Design15 each3Mar – MayWM1AB Mechatronics Sprint Project30
The first two blocks build the toolkit: circuits and motors, mechanics, professional skills, prototyping, microcontrollers and systems design. Block 3 puts it all together in a team project: design, build and test a robot for the end-of-year competition.
A typical block

Weeks 1–4: teaching. Each module usually has two lectures and a seminar a week, plus labs every other week.
Week 5: first assessment week, no teaching.
Weeks 6–7: more teaching and the last labs.
Week 9: second assessment week, for the reports.

How assessment works
Most modules have two assessments:























WeightUsuallyWhenA130%A timed computer-based test on campus (calculations plus short written answers), or a short individual portfolio or reportWeek 5 of the blockA270%A longer individual report, often built on the lab workWeek 9 of the block

You must pass every component, not just the module overall.
In the tests, a formula sheet is usually provided and only basic scientific calculators are allowed, so practise with the calculator you’ll use. Written working is often marked.
Group work in Blocks 2 and 3 is peer-assessed.
Each assessment brief says whether AI tools are allowed.

Study tips that have worked for me

Read the lab section of the brief before each lab, and photograph every reading. Your report depends on the data you take that day.
Finish every circuit calculation with a power balance and every kinematics answer with a units check.
Do the problem sets the week they’re set. The tests in week 5 cover everything from weeks 1–4.
